newsitem.title: USA: New Mexico legalizes Indian casinos.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico legalizes Indian casinos.

text.p: New Mexico Gov. Gary Johnson on Thursday approved a bill that legalizes Indian casinos but forces the state's tribes to share a bigger chunk of their gambling profits.

In a move that officials hoped would end a bitter two-year battle over gambling rights on Indian reservations, Johnson signed off on legislation that authorizes casinos on Indian land and gives the green light to video gambling machines at racetracks and fraternal orders.
Indian leaders said they were delighted that their casinos would be allowed to operate but immediately complained about the financial conditions legislators attached to the bill.

"We're very happy that this gaming bill passed," Frank Chaves, co-chairman of the New Mexico Indian Gaming Association said. "We're afraid, though, that some of the economic conditions contained in the bill may prove onerous to tribes."
Under the new legislation, tribes will be required to hand back 16 percent of revenues from gambling machines to the state and eventually pay for state regulation of the casinos.
Officials estimate those conditions would generate about $40 million a year in revenue for the state.

Previous gambling compacts signed between Johnson and New Mexico's 11 gaming tribes had called for 5 percent of gambling machine revenues to be shared with the state, but federal and state courts declared the agreements illegal, largely because they were not approved by the state legislature.

All but one of the 11 tribes have appealed to the United States Supreme Court to have the orignal compacts declared legal. Attorneys for the tribes said on Thursday they might be forced to accept the terms of the new legislation if their Supreme Court appeals fail.

Tribal leaders said they have spent millions of dollars building their casinos and gambling profits should go toward improving the quality of life on their dirt-poor reservations rather than filling state coffers.
The Justice Department forced a two-month shutdown of one casino last year but the others have remained open pending resolution of the dispute.
Should the tribes eventually accept the new legislation, the Department of the Interior would have the final say on whether the agreements are legal.
Off-reservation gambling at racetracks and fraternal orders cannot go ahead until the state and tribes reach final agreement on the terms of gambling compacts, officials said.
Gambling opponents, many of whom oppose gaming on social and moral grounds, said they would fight to block the new legislation before it takes effect.
"We hope to derail this thing before it gets all the way to being a law," Guy Clark, chairman of the New Mexico Coalition against Gambling said.
